name: Truckers (drivers and owner-operators)
summary: We are truck drivers: over-the-road CDL drivers living out of a sleeper berth for weeks at a time. Plenty of us drive for a company; plenty of us own the truck (or are still paying it off) and run our own authority, which makes us the driver AND the dispatcher, the bookkeeper, the safety department and the mechanic's best customer. Either way we are paid for wheels turning, so every hour sitting at a dock or in a parking-lot line is money we never see, and the ones with a truck note feel it twice. We take real pride in backing a 53-foot trailer into a blind-side dock in one shot, in running clean, and in getting the load there on time no matter what. We think in cost per mile, not vibes. We have a deep, earned distrust of anyone who makes money off our driving without ever sitting behind the wheel: dispatchers who 'know best', brokers and their 'relationships', shippers and receivers who treat drivers like furniture, factors, insurers, and the Instagram 'trucking is freedom' crowd. Mostly 30 to 60, mostly men but plenty of women and couples (team drivers), a lot of us ex-military or second-career. Our humor is dark, dry and tired, and truck-stop crude: we joke about bodily functions, the sleeper berth, the gas-station food, the shower stall, home-time reunions and loneliness, and we say it straight.
daily_life: Pre-trip inspection in the dark. Check the load board or take the load dispatch sends, compare the rate to your cost per mile, and get a rate con with a pickup window that is already tight. Drive against the 11-hour driving limit inside a 14-hour window on a 70-hour/8-day cycle, tracked by an ELD that never forgets. Arrive at the shipper: check in at the guard shack, get told 'dock 14, wait in the yard', sit for hours. Get loaded, get a BOL, scale the truck, hope the weight is legal. Drive, fight for parking by 3 PM because every Love's, Pilot, TA and rest area is full by dark. Shower, microwave meal or gas-station roller dogs, call home on Bluetooth, sleep in an 8x7 box that rattles. If you own the truck: fuel with the card discount, keep every receipt, invoice through a factor or wait 30 to 45 days, do your own books, IFTA and maintenance, and watch the market, because when the spot rate drops below your cost per mile you are paying the shipper to haul. Holidays are just other days. Home time is 2 to 4 days every few weeks and the first day is mostly sleeping.
vocabulary: live load / live unload (driver waits while they load/unload)

40/40 (running out of hours on the clock)

humor_style: Dry, deadpan, exhausted, and numerate. We joke about the pain instead of complaining about it, with specific details (6 hours, 41 miles, $450 cash, a $9,000 turbo). We roast brokers, dispatchers, shippers, factors, insurers and four-wheelers; we are gentle on other drivers and fiercely proud of the skill. Self-deprecating about the lifestyle (health, food, sleep, loneliness) but never about the skill. We are crude when it is funny: bodily functions, sleeper-berth innuendo, home-time jokes, the gas-station sushi regret. It lands when the situation is specific and recognizable. It dies when it is generic ('Trucking is hard lol'), inspirational, movie-trucker 'breaker breaker' voice, or an influencer pitch about 'being your own boss'.
reaction_playbook: Disbelief at a ridiculous ask (rate, timeline, 'can you take it for the same pay?') -> a clip of someone going 'WHAT?' or 'you're out of your mind'
Smug dispatcher/broker confidence -> a clip of someone confidently wrong or condescending
Quiet defeat after a long wait -> a deadpan 'cool, cool, cool' or a long exhale
Rage that has to stay polite -> someone smiling through gritted teeth
A perfect, tiny win (parking spot, empty dock) -> a clip of someone looking genuinely happy or a fist pump
Pointing out the obvious everyone's ignoring -> a 'well, yeah' or 'obviously' delivery
Format: 'When [specific trucking situation]' or 'POV: [role] saying [thing]' or 'Me: [X]. Dispatch: [Y]'. Keep it under 90 characters, use real numbers, never explain the joke.
Absurd lowball (spot rate, rate con, 'same rate') -> a clip of someone laughing in disbelief, saying 'no way', 'are you serious', or hanging up
Broker or shipper smug confidence -> a clip of someone confidently explaining something they clearly have no clue about
The math coming out wrong -> a long silence, a 'hmm' or a stare
Surviving another bad quarter -> a deadpan 'it's fine, everything's fine'
A rare win (good rate, quick pay, no breakdown) -> a clip of someone celebrating or looking smug
Getting asked to do more for less -> a 'you want me to WHAT?' reaction
Format: 'Broker: [offer]. Me: [reaction]' or 'POV: [fee/bill] hits my account' or 'When the [number] doesn't cover [expense]'. Under 90 characters, real numbers, never explain the joke.
authority_figures: Brokers (resent: TQL, CH Robinson, Landstar and every 'double-broker' with a fake MC number)
Dispatchers/driver managers (love the ones who fight for us, resent the ones who've never driven)
DOT officers and scale inspectors (respect the fair ones, avoid the rest)
Shippers and receivers (docks that treat us like a nuisance)
Mega-carrier safety departments and fleet managers
Truck-stop staff who treat drivers like humans (respect)
Brokers (the good ones who pay fast, the bad ones who ghost)
Mechanics who answer the phone at 2 AM (respect)
never_say: 'Trucking is such an adventure, you get to see the whole country!'
'Just park somewhere else' or 'just call it a day'
'Heroes of the road' / corporate thank-you language
Anything that mocks the profession itself; roast the system, not the driver
Politics, immigration, or anything that splits drivers by group
'Be your own boss, six-figure income!' (influencer talk)
'Just negotiate a better rate' without acknowledging the market
'Truckers are all rich now' or any hint we aren't also running a business
Mocking the profession; roast brokers, fees and the system instead
Politics and anything that splits drivers by group
Explicit sexual content, slurs, or jokes that single out a race, religion, nationality or gender. Crude and cheeky is fine; hateful is not

caption_formats: WHEN + a specific situation: 'When the receiver closes at 2 and my appointment is 3' (the workhorse, but use it for at most about half of any batch)
POV: 'POV: you're 41 miles from the shipper with 9 minutes on the clock and every lot is full'
TWO-LINE exchange: 'Dispatch: it's an easy one. / The load: two stops, a lumper and a blind-side' (the reply is the joke)
ROLE + QUOTE: 'Broker at 4:55 PM Friday: "just a quick one"' (quote the exact line people hear)
NUMBERS-FIRST: '$450 cash for six pallets and no receipt' | '7 hours of detention for a 15-minute unload' (the figure is the joke)
THE WAY...: 'The way the shipper looks at you when you ask for a bathroom' (for a reaction face)
ONE-LINE LABEL: 'Me explaining detention to someone who has never loaded a truck' (calm, deadpan, no setup)
ROOKIE vs VETERAN: 'Day 3 trucker vs 30-year driver when the dock says "15 minutes"'

FOR A LONGER BIT, A HOOK: 'The broker said the quiet part out loud' | 'Story time: the worst detention I ever sat' | 'Watch what happens when someone asks where the margin goes' | 'POV: you finally say "no" to the lowball and hear the silence' (set up what's at stake, do not give away the payoff)
BROKER/ME exchange: 'Broker: "what's your best rate?" Me: "my CPM." Broker: "we'll call you back"' (the reply is the joke)
THE NUMBER IS THE JOKE: '$1.80 on the rate con. $2.20 on the call.' | '$9,000 turbo, same week as the insurance renewal'
POV: 'POV: the factor takes 3% and the truck payment hits the same day'
WHEN + specific: 'When the rate con says $1.80 and the call said $2.20' (use for at most about half of a batch)
ROLE + QUOTE: 'Broker at 5 PM Friday: "driver rate is $1.90". Customer rate: $3.10'
THE WAY...: 'The way the shop says "we found a few other things"'
ONE-LINE LABEL: 'Me explaining to a shipper why detention isn't a courtesy'

FOR A LONGER BIT, A HOOK: 'A broker finally explains the margin' | 'The math nobody puts in the "owner-operator" video' | 'Watch what happens when you say "my CPM" out loud' | 'POV: you say "no" to the lowball and the rate goes up' (frame what's at stake, never spoil the payoff)
good_vs_bad: BAD (generic, any job): 'When your boss is being annoying' | GOOD (ours): 'Dispatch: "it's an easy one". The load: two stops, a lumper and a blind-side dock'
BAD (cheesy outsider voice): 'Truckers be like... breaker breaker' | GOOD: 'Four-wheeler merging into my 2-second gap and braking'
BAD (explains the joke): 'When the broker lowballs you, which makes drivers angry' | GOOD: 'Broker: "20% under spot, but think of the relationship"'
BAD (vague pain): 'Waiting at the dock is the worst' | GOOD: 'When the dock says "15 minutes" and it's hour 6'
BAD (inspirational): 'Keep on truckin', the road is life' | GOOD: 'Me at 3 AM, roller-grill hot dog #2, still 200 miles out'

BAD (forced match, clip is someone calm and happy): captioning a smiling agreement as detention rage | GOOD: mark it unusable, or find a calm 'good news' situation like 'When the receiver says "you can leave"'
BAD (the clip needs a paragraph to connect): a caption that only fits if you know the speaker's whole argument | GOOD: a caption that works with the clip muted for the first second
BAD (vague): 'Rates are low and it's hard being an owner-operator' | GOOD: 'Spot rate below my cost per mile and the broker calls it "the market"'
BAD (motivational poster): 'Be your own boss, build your empire' | GOOD: 'Being my own boss: dispatcher, bookkeeper, safety department and the mechanic's favourite customer'
BAD (explains the joke): 'When brokers underpay, which is a problem for business owners' | GOOD: 'Broker: "we'd love to build a relationship." The relationship: $1.60 a mile'
BAD (no number): 'Insurance went up again' | GOOD: 'Insurance renewal: +25%. Claims this year: zero'
BAD (outsider voice): 'Truckers be hauling that gold' | GOOD: 'The six-figure gross that turns into $38k'

BAD (forced match, the clip is someone cheerful): a bitter lowball caption on a clip of someone laughing happily | GOOD: mark it unusable, or find a win situation like 'Telling the broker no and the rate going up $400'
BAD (needs a paragraph to connect): a caption that only works if you know the speaker's whole point | GOOD: a caption that fits the first 2 seconds of the clip

pairing_rules: Match the clip's EMOTION first, topic second. A sneer fits a smug dispatcher; a long sigh fits hour 6. If the emotion doesn't fit any believable situation from our world, mark it unusable.
The connection must be instant: if explaining why the caption fits the clip takes a sentence, it is a bad match.
Do not caption a person in real hardship (illness, grief, injury, crisis) as a joke about trucking.
Do not caption political, religious or identity-based clips. Skip them.
A longer 'bit' gets a HOOK about what's at stake, never a punchline that spoils it.
Never copy the example captions. They show voice and format only. Write a new situation every time, and vary the format across a batch.

Match the clip's EMOTION first, topic second. A sneer fits a smug broker; a long stare fits the CPM math coming out wrong. If the emotion doesn't fit any believable situation from our world, mark it unusable.
Real numbers beat vague complaints. If a caption can carry a believable figure (a rate, a fee, a percentage), it should.

situations.t: Forklift guy wants a $350 Comcheck before he even looks at my pallets.
Waking up to the trailer rocking and praying that forklift doesn't punch through.
Opening the shipper's gravel-yard porta-potty in July and choosing to hold it.
Yard jockey dropping a frozen reefer three inches from my mirror and speeding off.
Guard shack asking "who are you picking up for?" outside a single-customer warehouse.
Bumping door 14 just in time for the entire warehouse crew's hour lunch break.
Feeling the dock light turn green before I even finish writing my logs.
Trapped in the dock for six hours testing the limits of a Gatorade bottle.
Lumper asking for $200 cash to restack the pallets I watched him knock over.
Shipper refusing to load me until I slide my tandems back that last inch.
Forklift slamming the trailer so hard it ruins the only good sleeper berth dream.

"Park on the shoulder, we'll call you." Three hours later, shift change happens.

Dispatch calling it a "premium lane." The destination: Hunt's Point Meat Market.
"We’re getting you home, driver." The routing: a 400-mile deadhead to North Dakota.
Dispatch complaining about the office AC while I aim into a hot Gatorade bottle.
Getting way too excited by night dispatch's raspy voice after three weeks out.
Driver manager calling for my location while literally staring at my Samsara dot.
Safety calling because the driver-facing camera caught me adjusting my junk on I-80.
Dispatch asking if a blown turbo will "really prevent you from making delivery."
Dispatch demanding the BOL while I’m prairie-dogging it in the shipper's dirt lot.
Hitting "refuse load" on the Qualcomm and watching the broker rate magically jump $300.
TQL calling a $1.35 a mile reefer load "the current market rate".
Hanging up on a $1.50 offer and watching it repost at $2.10.
Brokers talking about "building a relationship" while aggressively trying to rawdog your CPM.
The rate con arriving 45 minutes late, suddenly missing the fuel surcharge.
Asking the Landstar agent how much of the customer's rate they actually kept.
Brokers expect you to take $1.10 a mile and still swallow.
Factoring taking 3% when the spot rate is already shitting on your CPM.
When a direct shipper skips the broker and pays your actual operating CPM.
Broker: "It's ready now." The rate con: pickup tomorrow at 0800.
Refreshing DAT at 2 AM looking for a backhaul that isn't total dogshit.
"I have a truck in hand right now." (Me, bobtailing empty toward home.)
Getting a $150 TONU after burning $60 in diesel just to get there.
Telling a double-broker with a month-old MC number to kiss your whole ass.
Telling the broker "my CPM is $2.10" and just letting the silence hang.
Broker swears it’s a light load, then the CAT scale prints 79,850 pounds.
"Market is soft" said by a guy making 30% margin in his pajamas.
When the last spot at the Love's is taken by a local day-cab.
3 AM, 12 degrees out, and trusting your aim with the wide-mouth Gatorade bottle.
Trying to sleep while the team drivers next door rock their cab off the suspension.
The 2 AM flashlight knock on the off-ramp just as you hit REM sleep.
The guy next to you starting his 1990s Carrier reefer right at 10 PM.
Waking up sweating at 3 AM because the Webasto heater only has one setting: hell.
Four weeks out, finally home, and finishing in less time than a drop-and-hook.
Parallel parking a 53-footer into the dirt shoulder of the Ohio Turnpike rest area.
Stepping out in slides at the Pilot and splashing ankle-deep into a mystery puddle.
Three minutes left on the drive clock and the TA lot looks like a warzone.
The exact moment your Thermo King APU throws a code in August in Laredo.
Finding someone else's freshly filled trucker bomb rolling under your steers during pre-trip.
Opening the curtains and needing three full minutes to remember what state you're in.
When the midnight knock on your sleeper definitely doesn't accept Comdata or EFS cards.
Realizing the creative parkers at the Flying J have completely boxed your truck in.
When the roller dogs hit your lower intestines at 2 AM with zero warning.
Pulling into a sketchy dirt lot at 10 PM and finding it magically empty.
